title: 2026 Bespoked Dresden Picks 01: Forma, Leovelo, Manivelle, Sour, Streuner, Unicorn – Paul Kalifatidi & John Watson
content:
Guten morgen! We’re back in Saxony at the Flughafen Dresden for the 2026 Bespoked Dresden showcase. Paul and John spent the weekend at the world’s largest framebuilder showcase, selecting bikes to document for The Radavist’s coverage of the event. Check out our picks 01 from Forma, Leovelo, Manivelle, Sour, Streuner, and Unicorn below!

Sour and Hunt Ride Photos by Stefan Haehnel.

The Radavist thanks Brooks England for sponsoring our 2025 Bespoked Dresden coverage and our independent Reportage!

Forma Carbon Aluminum Lugged Gravel Bike – Paul Kalifatidi

One of the first conversations I had on Friday morning was with Jonathan Hornell-Kennedy of Forma Bicycles, formerly Frameworks. Jonathan makes his frames in Hamilton, Ontario where he winds his own carbon fiber tubes and CNCs his own aluminum lugs. While it is no secret that we love metal bikes, talking with Jonathan about carbon fiber and the building process made me more appreciative of the capabilities of the material.

I have always known that carbon fiber can be manipulated in a way that creates structural properties that metal cannot match, but I never fully understood the engineering itself. It isn’t as straightforward as more material here and less there; the direction of the carbon fibers themselves and their orientation in relation to other parts of the layup do a lot to dictate the behavior of the part. A uniform steel or titanium tube will bend equally in all directions. To make it stiffer in one direction, the wall thickness must be changed, and the shape must be changed. In carbon fiber, that is not the case, which is why it is such a fascinating material.

Carbon fiber is anisotropic, meaning its properties change based on fiber direction. Metal is isotropic, which means it has the same properties in all directions. You can change the compactness and direction of carbon fibers to change the strength of the material and how much it will flex under pressure. To show this, Jonathon had a seatpost suspended between two blocks. I could step on the tube and make it touch the ground, but then, after rotating it 90 degrees, it was now stiff enough to support my weight and not touch the ground. A tube will be more flexible if the fibers are laid closely together (like rings on a tube) and stiffer if the fibers are laid along the length of the tube. Jonathon tunes every tube, using fiber orientation and tube shape, to create a bike that flexes the way he would like it to: total control.

The carbon fiber tubes are held in the CNC aluminum lugs using an adhesive. The strength in the joint, Jonathan explained, is related to the thickness and uniformity of the adhesive surrounding the tube. In order to fit the tube into the lug, there is an intentional and precise loose fit. If the tube were simply inserted and gravity pulled it to the bottom of the lug, the joint would be weak. Instead, glass beads of a diameter that matches the gap between the tube and lug are mixed with the adhesive. They center the tube within the lug and ensure a strong joint. Again, I was fascinated. Following the theme of tight tolerances, even the bottom bracket has a trick up its sleeve.

Instead of using a BSA, T47, or even press-fit bearing cups, Jonathon uses Enduro bearings that are pressed directly into the aluminum lug. This eliminates multiple layers of material that could introduce play. He also designed the headset himself. The tolerance is so precise that by tightening the expansion nut within the steerer tube, it eliminates play, slippage, and twisting that can kink cables, along with dowels that help keep everything aligned.

This bike was built in full European spec with a Campagnolo drivetrain and wheels. Otherwise, everything pink is anodized aluminum that Jonathon made, including the stem and headset. While he doesn’t currently make a fork or handlebar, he is working on bringing even that in-house. Jonathon, thank you for explaining carbon fiber building methodology and material science in a palatable and easily digestible fashion. I loved every second of our conversation.

@FormaBike

Leovelo Gravel Bike with Paprika Bags – Paul Kalifatidi

Craftsmanship was on full display at the Leovelo stand: fascinating tube profiles and mesmerizing finishes were present on three bikes, and yet, I found the story behind this bike to be the most intriguing of all. John and I discussed the way to document a show. He told me, “Every bike and builder has a story that they have put on display, whether obviously or not, and it’s our job to find those stories and give them a flick into the world for people to read.”

And so, here’s the one that I loved the most from Bespoked Dresden: a Leovelo that wasn’t really made by Leo and a German tradition that goes back to the Medieval Times.

Leovelo is the brand of Leo Börger, a lovingly austere framebuilder with Bespoke’s best mullet. This bike is somewhat his, as it is his brand on the downtube, but most of the building was done by his friend, Valentine. Valentine is a journeyman bike mechanic and framebuilder. A journeyman, or Wandergeselle, in German, is a tradesperson who has completed their apprenticeship and basic training and now travels between different employers and places to develop their skills and learn from more master craftsmen. This tradition, though now much rarer, dates back to the Medieval Times. Now, there are only 500 Wandergeselle in Germany, including Valentine.

There are a number of rules and traditions that a journeyman must follow: The journey must last at least three years and one day, during which they must stay at least 50 kilometers away from their hometown. They must be under 30 years old, childless, and free of any debts. They are expected to come home with the same amount of money, generally a token amount, that they leave with, as they are forbidden from spending money on food or shelter. Instead, they trade their labor and skills in exchange for their needs. Valentine has also opted to forgo a phone to relinquish any reliance on technology. And lastly, they wear traditional clothing and have their ear pierced using a hammer and nail.

Leo was actually the very first Wandergeselle bike mechanic, and teaching Valentine to build this bike is a full-circle experience. Roland of Paprika made the bags for the bike. The name Paprika comes from Roland’s Hungarian roots, where spicy, not sweet, paprika is the traditional spice. On a bike, they add the necessary kick and flavor for adventure and aesthetics. This bike is stunning, in the brightest and most colorful way possible. Much like forgoing a phone, a Ratio conversion kit shifts a transmission drivetrain. The X-frame was inspired by the Mantis Valkyrie and other similar bikes. I also think that the shape of this frame helps hide the fact that these are 32-inch wheels.

It is stories like this one, where three men honored their cultural and personal heritage simply by making a bicycle, that makes shows like this special. Telling the stories is an honor.

@LeoveloFrameworks @PaprikaBags

Cycles Manivelle Basket Commuter – John Watson

One of my favorite European builders is Cycles Manivelle. Last year at Bespoked, I finally got to meet Silvin and the Manivelle team and documented an Effigear touring bike, so I was elated to see another practical, utilitarian build from the Strasbourg, France-based team this year. The project was commissioned by a doctor who rides between 30 and 50 kilometers a day visiting patients. He wanted a low-maintenance commuter with that Manivelle touch.

Silvin recalled the design process for the bike, focusing on designing a fork that would evoke emotions in the viewer. “For this fork, it was all about drawing on paper; I think I drew like 50 forks to find the design.” He was conflicted at first, stating that deviating from a traditional design can alter the visual language of a bicycle. Traditional design, particularly with forks, implies a perpetual forward motion.“I didn’t want the fork to give the impression of the bike going backward,” he commented. Silvin finally landed on a design which used the angle of the downtube to determine the strut of the fork.

Along this doctor’s commute are a few moments of respite found in secluded bike trails and single track. The client wanted a secure way to carry his bag and plenty of stopping power. Silvin designed the rack to be integrated into the truss fork and used a Manivelle direct-mount basket that attaches to the rack. For brakes, Trickstuff supplies the stopping power with 180 mm rotors.

For paint, the client wanted a Gulf Porsche Livery. Integrating the color blocking and design took a lot of mock-ups and sketching. The Cycles Manivelle painter is only 20 km from their workshop and traditionally paints motorcycles. He powder-coated the undercoat and wet-painted the logos on top before clear-coating it all.

Silvin, it was a pleasure to catch up with you and celebrate yet another stunning project.

@CyclesManivelle

Sour Bicycles 32er Pasta Party – John Watson

Christoph Süße’s Sour Bicycles always do things differently. The brand made a big splash over here at The Radavist with its Double Choc and Cowboy Cookie full suspension bikes, but Chris’ heart lies in the humble singlespeed, rigid mountain bike. Wanting a sweet taste of the 32er fad, Chris set out to design the ultimate Pasta Party 32er. Rather than scaling up the design 10% from the 29er chassis to a 32er, including the suspension-corrected 29er fork, he designed an all-new 32er suspension-corrected fork.

Why go through all this extra effort? Chris believes the 32er platform will be here to stay and that more suspension options will be offered in the coming years. He wants his customers to have the option of putting a suspension fork on the Pasta Party 32er, and in order to do that, the bike needs a special rigid fork.

This is very much the Sour modus operandi. Take the existing model, question it, and design something better, resulting in a project that takes a little bit more effort, but the result is the reward for Chris. Take, for instance, his UDH post mount brake. Rather than making the brake mount attach to the seat stays, it fits between the hub axle and dropout face, creating a clean material break and the opportunity to design a beautiful brake mount.

Single-speed fans will want to know his setup. On this bike, he’s running a Boone cog and a Cyber Cycles spacer kit, which was Cyber’s first product from over twenty years ago. Chris is a big fan of what Cyber Cycles produces.

Chris, stay sweet, buddy. Hope you heal up fast!

@SourBicycles

Streuner GT 98 Karakoram – John Watson

Bicycle design and fabrication are often by-products of collaborative efforts. Especially in Europe, where many brands work together to solve problems. Often, a creative person operates in the artistic realm, while an engineer keeps the project grounded.

That’s the case with the Köln, Germany-based Streuner and this GT 32er. Joe Streuner and Sami Al-Khayat worked together on this unique project. Joe explained that the bike’s inspiration began with the fork crown. “We started talking about it in May. It started with the fork crown. We realized the crown design could allow for fork blades of any length, so why not 32er?” The design process is often Joe sketching wild ideas and Sami saying either they will work or won’t. Sami interrupts to add a perfect metaphor: “Joe’s the gas pedal, and I’m the brake.”

This project, as it turns out, was all gas. Once Joe designed the fork, he took his 1998 GT Karakoram and began to sketch out design possibilities. Inspired by the triple triangle, Joe began to draw a series of waves, rippling up the frame.

Following the lines of the triple triangle, the angle of each of these waves is a reflection of that angle. Then, when the double top tube took shape, the lines of it also reflected the lines of the seat stays. Furthering the conceptual ideas, the two flattened a tandem tube and brazed it to the seat tube, allowing the internal routing to mass into it on either side of the head tube.

Taking the sketch of the waves, the two pinged their friend at Kernig to design a stem that would follow the same parti design. What’s perhaps the most outstanding part of this whole project is that, from start to finish, it only took a week to complete. Well done, team!

@Streuner @AltelierWolken @BurakGueller @KernigComp

Heintz Fundamentalist with Intend BC Unicorn – John Watson

Felix from Intend BC was wearing a shirt that simply said “Unicorn” on it. Thinking Unicorn was the name of the full-suspension bike he was standing next to, I began to ask about the bike, leading to the realization that Unicorn was the new Intend special projects label. Earlier that day, I began following this skunkworks side label on Instagram.

Intend BC is a small manufacturer based in Freiburg, Germany. The brand gets flooded with requests from customers and shops for special finishes, colored anodizing, and the like. The small team at Intend can now make small batches of forks, shocks, stems, and brakes in unique colors and finishes and sell them under the Unicorn label, oftentimes directly to consumers.

For the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show, the Unicorn team took a Heintz Fundamentalist 160/160 titanium full suspension bike and began to play with complementary anodization of the shock and fork to the titanium finish. With hits of purple in the Rover Monocoque shock, Grace stem, Trinity brakes, and Edge World Cup fork, the result is nothing short of show-stopping and amazing.

Intend’s products epitomize German engineering. The carbon uppers of the Edge World Cup fork, impeccable machine paths throughout the parts, and finishing tones are nothing short of amazing. Eagle-eyed Intend fans will note the new design of the brake caliper with aluminum cooling fins.

The Radavist might not be a core MTB website, but Felix is a big fan of what we do over here. It was great to get to chat with you, Felix. Finding fellow riders at bike shows is what it’s all about!

@UnicornByIntend @HeintzBikes
